title: Sleep Calculator: how it works, formula and examples
excerpt: Sleep Calculator: Best bedtimes and wake-up times based on 90-minute sleep cycles. Learn how to use it, the formula behind it, a worked example and answers to…
content:
The [Sleep Calculator](/sleep-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Best bedtimes and wake-up times based on 90-minute sleep cycles. Enter your i want to…, time (24-hour, e.g. 07:00) and sleep cycles and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Find the best time to go to bed or wake up, based on 90-minute sleep cycles. Sleep runs in cycles of light sleep, deep sleep and dreaming, each lasting about 90 minutes — waking up at the end of a cycle feels far better than being woken in the middle of deep sleep. The calculator works backwards from your alarm time (or forwards from your bedtime) in whole cycles, and allows about 14 minutes to fall asleep. Most adults need 5 cycles (7.5 hours) a night. This is an estimate for healthy adults, not medical advice. It does not suit children, pregnancy, eating disorders or anyone with a medical condition — talk to a doctor or registered dietitian before changing your diet or sleep habits.

## How to use the Sleep Calculator

Start by choosing your i want to… from the list, then typing or pasting your time (24-hour, e.g. 07:00) and finally entering your sleep cycles. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Choose whether you want to wake at a set time or fall asleep at a set time.
2. Enter the time and how many sleep cycles you want (5 is the usual choice).
3. Pick a bedtime or wake-up time from the list — each is a whole number of cycles.

## Formula

Each sleep cycle lasts about 90 minutes. Bedtime = wake-up time − (cycles × 90 minutes) − 14 minutes to fall asleep. Wake-up time = bedtime + 14 minutes + (cycles × 90 minutes). Five cycles is 7.5 hours of sleep.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Sleep Calculator](/sleep-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. To wake at 7:00 AM with 5 sleep cycles (7.5 hours), go to bed at 11:16 PM: 7:00 AM minus 7.5 hours is 11:30 PM, minus 14 minutes to fall asleep gives 11:16 PM. Try the same figures in the [Sleep Calculator](/sleep-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (I want to…: Wake up at a set time, Time (24-hour, e.g. 07:00): 07:00, Sleep cycles: 5), the [Sleep Calculator](/sleep-calculator) returns Go to bed at: 6 cycles (9 h) — 9:46 PM 5 cycles (7.5 h) — 11:16 PM 4 cycles (6 h) — 12:46 AM, Best choice: 11:16 PM for 5 cycles (7.5 hours of sleep), Time to fall asleep: About 14 minutes is already allowed for. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [BMI Calculator](/bmi-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## Why waking mid-cycle feels terrible

Each 90-minute cycle moves from light sleep into deep sleep and then dreaming (REM). Waking during deep sleep leaves you groggy and confused for up to half an hour — sleep inertia. Waking at the end of a cycle, in light sleep, feels much easier, even if you slept slightly less. That is why 7.5 hours (5 cycles) often feels better than 8 hours (5 cycles plus a third of a cycle).

## How much sleep do you need?

Most adults need 7–9 hours, which is 5–6 cycles. Teenagers need more (8–10 hours), older adults a little less. The cycles matter more than the exact total: a regular bedtime and wake-up time, a dark cool room, and no screens for the last half hour do more for sleep quality than chasing an extra 20 minutes. If you regularly need an alarm to wake, you are probably not getting enough.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Aim for 5 cycles (7.5 hours) — 6 cycles (9 hours) if you are still tired.
- Keep the same bedtime and wake-up time every day, weekends included.
- Allow 14 minutes to fall asleep — the calculator already does.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long is a sleep cycle?

About 90 minutes. Each cycle moves from light sleep into deep sleep and then dreaming (REM), and the cycle repeats through the night. Try it with your own numbers in the [Sleep Calculator](/sleep-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How many sleep cycles do I need?

Most adults need 5 cycles (7.5 hours) a night; 6 cycles (9 hours) is better if you are still tired. Teenagers need more. If you are unsure about a value, try a rough figure first and then refine it — the result updates instantly.

### Why do I feel worse after 8 hours than after 7.5?

Because 8 hours is 5 cycles plus a third of a cycle — the alarm can catch you in deep sleep. 7.5 hours ends at a cycle boundary, in light sleep, which feels much easier. Try it with your own numbers in the [Sleep Calculator](/sleep-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What time should I go to bed to wake at 7 AM?

For 5 cycles (7.5 hours), 11:16 PM — 7:00 AM minus 7.5 hours, minus about 14 minutes to fall asleep. Try it with your own numbers in the [Sleep Calculator](/sleep-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
